disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent, distressing preoccupation with perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear minor to others. Individuals often engage in repetitive behaviors (e.g., mirror checking, comparing, grooming, camouflaging) or mental acts in response to these concerns, which consume significant time and cause functional impairment. The onset is typically in adolescence and the course tends to be chronic, with exacerbations linked to social evaluation, appearance-focused contexts, or stress; insight can range from good to delusional. BDD is distinguished from normal appearance concerns and from eating disorders by the intensity of the preoccupation, the degree of impairment, and the focus on specific perceived defects rather than primarily on weight or body shape.

narrative.stressor: Terri’s appearance concerns intensified after she started working more independently on university conventions, where she frequently had to be on-site, visible to large groups, and included in marketing photos and social media posts about the events. Her habit of photographing everything for work and for her own prairie photography gradually shifted from documenting others to scrutinizing herself in every candid shot, especially when coworkers tagged her in group photos online. Over the course of a year, she began turning down opportunities to be the face of eco-friendly initiatives or to present at planning meetings, and she rearranged event schedules to avoid being in front of cameras, which frustrated colleagues and jeopardized her reliability. She finally agreed to see a mental health professional after her supervisor gently confronted her about missed planning sessions and her parents noticed she was backing out of community activities she used to love, despite insisting nothing was wrong except that she "looked terrible in every photo."
narrative.chief_complaint: I can’t stop fixating on how bad I look in every picture and it’s starting to interfere with my work and social life.

narrative.stressor: For Eduardo, long-standing self-consciousness about his appearance worsened when teammates on his soccer club began posting high-resolution game photos and workout videos to promote the league on social media. Seeing himself frozen in action shots at the gym and on the field, and comparing those images to fitness influencers he followed, made him increasingly preoccupied with how he looked from specific angles during play and dancing at salsa nights. Over time, he began arriving early to the gym and staying late to inspect himself in mirrors and adjust his clothing, and he started avoiding group photos and social events where he might be tagged online, which friends noticed as out of character for someone usually so sociable. He eventually sought psychiatric help after skipping several matches and salsa nights in a row, and his sister urged him to talk to a professional when she realized he was reorganizing his entire schedule around avoiding being seen in ways he felt made him "look wrong."
narrative.chief_complaint: I spend so much time checking and rechecking how I look at the gym and before going out that it’s taking over my days.

narrative.stressor: Leyda’s concerns about her appearance became more pronounced in the years surrounding perimenopause, as subtle age-related changes coincided with her children becoming more independent and her taking on a more public-facing role at the law office. Being introduced as the experienced paralegal at community workshops for immigrant families meant standing under bright lights, appearing in firm newsletters, and occasionally being in group photos, all of which heightened her focus on perceived flaws she felt were "showing more with age." She gradually started declining speaking opportunities, rearranging her schedule to avoid video calls, and spending increasing time getting ready for work, which her husband and coworkers noticed as a shift from her previously practical, low-fuss routines. She agreed to see a clinician after missing a book club meeting and a community-center workshop she had organized because she felt she "couldn’t let anyone see" her that day, and her primary care physician, noting the impact on her functioning despite normal physical exams, recommended a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: Lately I can’t stop dwelling on how my face and body look as I’m aging, and it’s making me avoid things I used to do without thinking.
